subject: Request: reserved GPU queueing exemption for latency-critical inference
messages:
From: Olivia Zhang <olivia.zhang@nimbusrail.com>
To: camila.reyes@redwood.com
Date: 2027-10-04T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Request: reserved GPU queueing exemption for latency-critical inference

Hi Camila,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the team and I are excited about Redwood Dedicated. One follow-up ask from our SRE/real-time team: for a small reserved GPU pool we want an "exemption" from the standard queueing behavior during our peak windows.

Context: NimbusRail runs a real-time anomaly detection pipeline for signalling systems. During dispatch-critical events we need sub-50ms tail latency for a small subset of calls (~5-10 qps) and cannot tolerate typical queueing backpressure caused by long-running batch jobs that are colocated in the same reserved pool.

What we're asking: can Redwood grant a temporary queueing/preemption carve-out for our reserved pool during our peak window (08:00–20:00 PDT), where latency-critical requests get priority sockets that bypass the normal inflight queue for up to 30k tokens/day? We're happy to accept a cost uplift for dedicated low-latency reservation and to sign an addendum that limits the carve-out to our production pool.

Attached is a short SLO diagram and our basic traffic profile. We're trying to understand implementation options and any commercial/legal constraints before we commit. Can you advise next steps and who we should loop in?

Thanks,
Olivia Zhang
Director of SRE, NimbusRail

Forwarding Olivia's note — high priority ask from NimbusRail (deal NR-2027-114). Quick summary: they want a limited carve-out that lets a tiny percentage of calls bypass the standard queueing/backpressure in their reserved pool during 08:00–20:00 PDT. They expect ~5-10 qps and are willing to pay a premium and sign an addendum.

Questions I have for you both:
- Ben: commercial/contracting — is this something we can accommodate in an MSA addendum? Any precedent on credits/penalties if carve-outs cause noisy-neighbor regressions?
- Karthik: technical — what are the simplest options we can operate/support without heavy runtime changes? Can we do token-based priority ingress, or is this a dedicated lane that requires a different reservation type?
- Naomi: legal — will we be comfortable with an exception that changes queueing semantics? Any language we should avoid (e.g., "guarantee" vs "priority" vs "best-effort")?

I've attached a short one-pager with their profile and a suggested commercial approach. If we can give them a clear implementation path + timeline, Olivia is ready to escalate internally.

Camila Reyes
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Fwd: Request: reserved GPU queueing exemption for latency-critical inference

Camila — thanks for the ping and Olivia — appreciate the detail. High-level technical assessment:

1) Feasible approaches (ordered by implementation risk):
   - Option A (low-risk): Deploy a small dedicated "latency lane" inside the customer's Dedicated pool that uses strict admission control (token bucket) and a separate lightweight scheduler. Latency calls go to that lane and have isolated kv-cache and preemptible capacity. This requires configuration only — no kernel changes.
   - Option B (medium-risk): Priority ingress where we tag requests and allow them to bypass the per-GPU inflight queue until a hard cap. This is trickier: we need to ensure KV cache correctness and that memory pressure from the bypass doesn't impact other tenants.
   - Option C (high-risk): Separate physical reservation or separate instance class for the lane (recommended if budget allows).

2) Tradeoffs:
   - Latency lane provides the cleanest SLO isolation but increases unit cost (extra reserved vgpu fraction).
   - Priority ingress reduces cost but requires runtime safeguards and careful monitoring to avoid tail regressions.

3) Operational controls we should include:
   - Auto-failover to normal queueing if memory or GPU utilization exceeds safety thresholds.
   - Daily crediting policy for any SLO misses attributable to our changes.
   - Canary rollout (48–72h) and a one-week validation window.

I attached a short tech assessment and rough ETA: Option A could be enabled in ~7–10 business days if we provision a small dedicated lane; Option B would need ~3–4 weeks of runtime changes and testing.

Requested inputs:
- Ben: commercial tolerance for the daily crediting policy?
- Naomi: suggested legal phrasing for "priority" vs "guarantee" and any limits around regulatory language.

Karthik
Senior Product Engineer, Serving Runtime
Attachment: tech-assessment.xlsx
From: camila.reyes@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Request: reserved GPU queueing exemption for latency-critical inference — proposed next steps

Hi Olivia — thanks for the clarity. Summarizing our proposed path and asks so we can move to a written addendum: 

1) Technical approach: we propose Option A — a small dedicated latency lane inside your reserved pool. This isolates latency-critical events and keeps impact on other workloads minimal. Karthik's team estimates a 7–10 business day turnaround for provisioning + 48–72h canary.

2) Commercial/legal: as discussed, this will be an addendum to your Dedicated contract limiting the carve-out to the production pool and to the hours 08:00–20:00 PDT. We'll include a daily crediting policy for measurable SLO misses attributable to the carve-out. Naomi — can you draft conservative language that avoids "guarantee" and uses "priority admission" and "SLO crediting"?

3) Next steps for NimbusRail: please confirm:
   - Exact peak windows (we have 08:00–20:00 PDT as your ask)
   - Confirmation of expected qps on the latency lane (est. 5–10 qps)
   - Approval to sign the MSA addendum (we'll send a DocuSign link once legal approves)

If you confirm today/tomorrow we can provision the lane and begin the canary the week after next. I'll copy Ben for the commercial terms and Karthik for delivery.

Camila Reyes
